questions.q: A 35-year-old farmer presents with a painless ulcer on his right hand that started as a papule after a scratch from a thorn. The ulcer has a necrotic black eschar in the center with surrounding non-pitting edema. Blood culture grows Gram-positive spore-forming rods. Which virulence factor is most responsible for the edema seen in this case?
questions.exp: Anthrax cutaneous infection (Bacillus anthracis). Edema toxin = Protective antigen (PA) + Edema factor (EF); EF is an adenylate cyclase that raises cAMP, causing edema. Lethal toxin (PA + LF) causes macrophage lysis. The poly-D-glutamic acid capsule inhibits phagocytosis but is not responsible for edema.

questions.q: A 28-year-old immunocompetent woman has a 3-cm well-demarcated ring-shaped scaly plaque on the scalp with broken-off hairs at the margin ('dot' pattern on dermoscopy). KOH preparation shows spores arranged in chains outside the hair shaft. Which organism is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Ectothrix (spores outside hair shaft in chains) is caused by Microsporum canis (large-spored ectothrix) and M. audouinii. Trichophyton tonsurans and T. violaceum cause endothrix (spores inside shaft, black-dot pattern). T. schoenleinii causes favus (scutula, not chains).

questions.q: A 22-year-old male presents with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base on the glans penis for 3 days, preceded by burning and tingling. Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells. He had a similar episode 4 months ago. The drug of choice for long-term suppression to prevent recurrences is:
questions.exp: For suppressive therapy of recurrent genital herpes, Valacyclovir 500 mg once daily is standard. Acyclovir 400 mg BD is also used for suppression. The options given for episodic therapy (TDS for 5 days, 1-day regimen) are not suppressive regimens. Cidofovir is for acyclovir-resistant HSV.

questions.q: A 25-year-old sex worker presents with a painless, clean-based, indurated ulcer on the labia majora of 10 days' duration. Gram stain of ulcer exudate reveals no organisms. Dark-field microscopy shows motile corkscrew-shaped organisms. VDRL is reactive at 1:8. The best drug for treatment is:
opts: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose
questions.exp: Primary syphilis (Treponema pallidum) — treatment of choice is Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose. Doxycycline × 14 days is used in penicillin allergy. Azithromycin has been used but resistance is reported. Ceftriaxone is an alternative but not first-line.

questions.q: On routine examination, a 40-year-old male presents with hypopigmented anesthetic patches on the trunk and thickened greater auricular and ulnar nerves. Slit-skin smear is negative. The lepromin test is strongly positive. Which type of leprosy is this?
questions.exp: Tuberculoid leprosy (TT): few (1-5) well-defined, hypopigmented, anesthetic patches; thickened named nerve trunks; negative smear (paucibacillary); strongly positive lepromin (Mitsuda) reaction indicating strong CMI. Lepromatous is lepromin-negative, smear-positive, multiple lesions.

questions.q: A 30-year-old leprosy patient on multidrug therapy (MDT) develops sudden onset facial edema, erythema and tenderness of existing lesions, fever, and peripheral nerve pain with new motor deficit. ESR is elevated. This reaction is classified as:
questions.exp: Type 1 (reversal) reaction is a delayed-type hypersensitivity (Type IV) response occurring in borderline leprosy. It features sudden edema and erythema of existing skin lesions, acute neuritis with new nerve deficit, and constitutional symptoms. ENL (Type 2) presents with tender subcutaneous nodules and is immune-complex mediated (Type III), occurring in LL/BL.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with malar rash, photosensitivity, alopecia, oral ulcers, and arthralgia. ANA is positive (1:640, homogeneous pattern). Anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm antibodies are positive. The cutaneous manifestation most specific to this condition is:
questions.exp: The malar (butterfly) rash — erythema over the cheeks sparing the nasolabial folds — is the hallmark specific cutaneous feature of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Anti-Sm is specific for SLE as a serological marker, but the malar rash is the skin finding most characteristic of SLE. Discoid plaques occur in DLE which is chronic cutaneous lupus.

questions.q: A 50-year-old male presents with progressive dysphagia, Raynaud's phenomenon, mat-like telangiectasias on the fingers, pitting scars on the fingertips, and hidebound skin extending to the shoulders. ANA shows anti-Scl-70 positivity. Which pattern of systemic sclerosis does this represent and what complication should be screened for?
questions.exp: Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) is associated with diffuse cutaneous SSc with truncal skin involvement. Diffuse SSc is strongly associated with interstitial lung disease (ILD). Anti-centromere antibody is associated with limited SSc (CREST) and pulmonary arterial hypertension. Renal crisis occurs in diffuse SSc but is not the primary screening target with anti-Scl-70.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with flaccid bullae on normal-appearing skin that rupture easily leaving denuded areas. Nikolsky sign is positive. DIF shows IgG and C3 in a net-like (fishnet) pattern around epidermal cells. ELISA confirms antibodies against desmoglein 3. The diagnosis and the level of split are:
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris: flaccid bullae, positive Nikolsky sign, DIF showing IgG in intercellular (fishnet/chicken-wire) pattern, antibodies against Dsg3 (mucous membranes) ± Dsg1 (skin). The split is suprabasal intraepidermal (acantholysis above the basal layer). Pemphigus foliaceous has subcorneal split and Dsg1 antibodies only.

questions.q: A 70-year-old diabetic male presents with tense bullae on inflamed urticarial bases on the inner thighs and abdomen. Nikolsky sign is negative. DIF shows linear IgG and C3 at the basement membrane zone. The antigen target is most likely:
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid: tense bullae on inflamed base, negative Nikolsky, linear IgG/C3 at BMZ on DIF. Antigens are BP180 (BPAG2) in the hemidesmosomal region and BP230 (BPAG1). Type VII collagen is the antigen in epidermolysis bullosa acquisita. Laminin 332 is targeted in mucous membrane pemphigoid.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man presents with a pearly white nodule with rolled borders and central ulceration on the nasal tip. He reports years of sun exposure. Dermoscopy shows arborizing vessels and spoke-wheel structures. The most appropriate first-line treatment for this lesion if limited to the face with well-defined margins is:
opts: Wide local excision with 5 mm margins
questions.exp: Nodular basal cell carcinoma on the nose (high-risk H-zone) — Mohs micrographic surgery is the gold standard for high-risk BCCs on the face (H-zone, recurrent, ill-defined, large). It offers tissue-sparing excision with complete margin assessment. Standard excision with 4-5 mm margins is used for low-risk lesions. Cryotherapy is for superficial BCC.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male presents with a rapidly growing, well-differentiated keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma 2.5 cm in diameter on the lower lip with palpable ipsilateral submandibular lymphadenopathy. AJCC staging and the primary surgical treatment would be:
opts: Stage T2N0M0; wide local excision alone
Stage T2N1M0; wide local excision + neck dissection ± adjuvant RT
Stage T1N1M0; imiquimod + sentinel node biopsy
questions.exp: Lip SCC ≥2 cm but <4 cm = T2; clinically palpable ipsilateral node = N1; no metastasis = M0. T2N1M0 requires wide local excision with adequate margins plus ipsilateral neck dissection; adjuvant radiotherapy is indicated for perineural invasion, positive nodes, or close margins. Imiquimod is not used for invasive SCC with nodes.

questions.q: A 45-year-old gardener presents with a verrucous nodule on the right foot that developed after a penetrating injury with a wood splinter 6 months ago. Histology shows 'copper penny' bodies (Medlar bodies / sclerotic cells). The causative organisms belong to which group?
questions.exp: Chromoblastomycosis is caused by dematiaceous (melanized) fungi — Fonsecaea pedrosoi (most common), Cladophialophora carrionii, Phialophora verrucosa. The pathognomonic finding is Medlar bodies (muriform/sclerotic cells — copper penny bodies). Mycetoma has grains (no sclerotic cells). Sporotrichosis shows asteroid bodies, not Medlar bodies.

questions.q: A 32-year-old HIV-positive patient (CD4 count 80 cells/μL) presents with hyperkeratotic, crusted plaques on the hands, feet, scalp, and periungual areas. More than 2 million mites are found on skin scraping. The drug of choice for this condition is:
opts: Oral ivermectin 200 μg/kg + topical keratolytics (repeated doses)
questions.exp: Norwegian (crusted) scabies in an immunocompromised host requires combination therapy: oral ivermectin (multiple doses on days 1, 2, 8, 9, 15) plus topical keratolytics (5% salicylic acid) to remove crusts and permethrin. Single-dose ivermectin is insufficient. All close contacts must be treated simultaneously.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with an annular plaque with central clearing and a sharply defined scaly edge on the groin. The plaque is intensely pruritic and worsens in summer. KOH preparation shows septate hyphae. She has been using a topical steroid provided by a local pharmacist, which has made the lesion larger. This condition is best described as:
opts: Tinea cruris modified by topical steroid (tinea incognito)
questions.exp: Tinea incognito: dermatophyte infection modified by corticosteroid use, resulting in atypical, enlarged, less scaly plaques. The clinical appearance is altered but KOH remains positive for septate hyphae. Erythrasma shows coral-red fluorescence under Wood's lamp (Corynebacterium). Candidal intertrigo has satellite pustules and budding yeast on KOH.

questions.q: A 19-year-old presents with comedones, inflammatory papules, and a few nodules on the face and trunk for 2 years. He has failed two courses of topical retinoids and oral doxycycline. He now asks about isotretinoin. Before initiating therapy, the mandatory baseline investigation in this patient is:
opts: Liver function tests and fasting lipid profile
Pregnancy test (if female) and fasting lipid profile
questions.exp: Before isotretinoin, mandatory baseline investigations include liver function tests and fasting lipid profile (triglycerides and cholesterol) because isotretinoin can cause hypertriglyceridemia and hepatotoxicity. In females of childbearing potential, a pregnancy test (urine or serum β-hCG) is mandatory due to teratogenicity. CBC is also recommended in some guidelines.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male with plaque psoriasis not responding to methotrexate is started on a biologic targeting IL-17A. After 3 months, he develops oral candidiasis and later a new-onset Crohn's-like flare. Which biologic was most likely prescribed?
questions.exp: Secukinumab (anti-IL-17A) is associated with increased risk of mucocutaneous candidiasis (IL-17 is important for anti-fungal immunity at mucosae) and has been shown to worsen inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). This distinguishes it from TNF inhibitors, which can treat IBD. IL-23 inhibitors (guselkumab, risankizumab) do not carry the same IBD risk.

questions.q: A 40-year-old female presents with pruritic, polygonal, flat-topped, violaceous papules on the flexor aspect of the wrists and ankles. Wickham's striae are visible. Oral mucosa shows white reticulate streaks. Histology shows a sawtooth pattern of rete ridges with a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Lichen planus: the 6 P's — Pruritic, Polygonal, Planar (flat-topped), Purple, Papules/Plaques at Penultimate sites (wrists, ankles). Wickham's striae, oral involvement, sawtooth rete ridges with band-like lymphocytic infiltrate hugging the DEJ (interface dermatitis), and civatte bodies are characteristic.

questions.q: A 25-year-old male presents with symmetric, sharply demarcated silvery scaly plaques on the extensor surfaces of elbows and knees, and scalp. Auspitz sign is positive. He also has nail pitting. His HLA type associated with early onset disease is:
questions.exp: HLA-Cw6 is the strongest genetic association with psoriasis, particularly psoriasis type 1 (early onset, <40 years, positive family history). HLA-B27 is associated with psoriatic arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis. HLA-DR4 is associated with rheumatoid arthritis. HLA-B13 has weaker associations.

questions.q: A 30-year-old male presents with 6-month history of multiple grouped papulovesicular lesions on elbows, knees, and scalp. DIF of perilesional skin shows granular IgA deposits at the tips of dermal papillae. He also has bloating and loose stools. The association with which condition explains his gastrointestinal symptoms?
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH): IgA deposits at dermal papillary tips on DIF is pathognomonic. DH is the cutaneous manifestation of coeliac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy); nearly all patients have HLA-DQ2/DQ8 and anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies. Gluten-free diet improves both skin and bowel symptoms.

questions.q: A 65-year-old male presents with a rapidly enlarging plum-colored plaque on the leg over 3 months. He is HIV-positive with CD4 count of 120 cells/μL. Histology shows spindle cells, slit-like vascular spaces, and extravasated red cells. HHV-8 immunostaining is positive. The recommended treatment for widespread skin disease is:
questions.exp: AIDS-related Kaposi's sarcoma: HHV-8 associated, spindle cells with slit-like vascular spaces. For widespread/systemic disease, combination of ART (which raises CD4 and reduces HHV-8 replication) plus systemic chemotherapy — liposomal doxorubicin (pegylated) is first-line for advanced KS. Intralesional vinblastine is for limited lesions only.

questions.q: A 45-year-old male presents with a Wood's lamp examination revealing an ash-leaf-like hypopigmented macule, a shagreen patch, and periungual fibromas. He has a history of seizures since childhood and mild intellectual disability. The inheritance pattern and the gene most commonly mutated are:
questions.exp: Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC): autosomal dominant inheritance. TSC1 (hamartin, chromosome 9q) and TSC2 (tuberin, chromosome 16p) mutations; TSC2 is more common and associated with more severe disease. Cutaneous features: ash-leaf macules (hypopigmented, under Wood's lamp), shagreen patches, periungual fibromas (Koenen's tumors), facial angiofibromas.

questions.q: During a Punch biopsy, after removing a 4mm punch, the dermatologist should close the wound with a suture. For a punch biopsy on the back, the correct orientation of the elliptical wound closure to minimize tension is to align the long axis along:
questions.exp: Wounds should be closed along relaxed skin tension lines (RSTLs) to minimize tension, reduce scarring, and achieve better cosmesis. RSTLs are formed by the orientation of the underlying musculature and are perpendicular to the direction of muscle pull. Langer's lines (lines of cleavage) are based on cadaver studies and are less clinically relevant than RSTLs for wound orientation.

questions.q: A 22-year-old female presents with recurrent sun-exposed photosensitivity, diffuse hyperpigmentation, pellagra-like dermatitis, and neuropsychiatric symptoms. She is from a low-income group. Urinary amino acid chromatography shows generalized neutral aminoaciduria. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Hartnup disease: autosomal recessive defect in neutral amino acid transporter (SLC6A19) affecting intestinal and renal absorption of tryptophan (and other neutral AAs). Reduced tryptophan → reduced niacin → pellagra-like picture (dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia) triggered by sun exposure. Neutral aminoaciduria is diagnostic. Pellagra proper is nutritional niacin deficiency without aminoaciduria.

questions.q: A 38-year-old male presents with slowly progressive, yellowish-brown hyperkeratosis of the palms and soles with constricting bands around the digits. The bands are gradually amputating the little finger. He has a strong family history. Which condition is this and what is the mode of inheritance?
questions.exp: Vohwinkel syndrome (keratoderma hereditaria mutilans): diffuse palmoplantar keratoderma with starfish-shaped keratotic plaques on dorsa of hands/feet and honeycomb keratoderma, plus pseudoainhum (constricting bands causing autoamputation of digits). Autosomal dominant; caused by GJB2 (connexin 26) mutations. Mal de Meleda is AR, transgressively spreading. Papillon-Lefèvre is AR with periodontitis.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male presents with multiple flesh-colored to hyperpigmented macules and patches in sun-protected areas, with woody hardness of overlying skin. He also has calcinosis cutis and Raynaud's phenomenon. Anti-centromere antibody is positive. The classification of this disease and its most feared long-term complication are:
opts: Limited SSc (CREST syndrome); pulmonary arterial hypertension
Mixed connective tissue disease; renal crisis
questions.exp: CREST syndrome (Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasias) = limited systemic sclerosis. Anti-centromere antibody is the hallmark. The most feared life-threatening complication is pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). ILD is more common in diffuse SSc with anti-Scl-70. Renal crisis is associated with diffuse SSc.

questions.q: A 4-year-old boy develops vesicles and pustules at the hairline and on the trunk 2 days after his sibling had chickenpox. The lesions are in different stages of development. This finding of lesions in different stages at the same time is called:
questions.exp: Varicella (chickenpox): characteristic feature is pleomorphism (polymorphism) — lesions in different stages (macules, papules, vesicles, pustules, crusts) present simultaneously at the same time in the same area. This distinguishes it from smallpox where all lesions are at the same stage. Centrifugal distribution is seen in smallpox.

questions.q: A 30-year-old male presents with painless, smooth, 1-cm papules with a central dell (umbilication) on the trunk and genital area. He is HIV positive with CD4 count of 50 cells/μL. He has more than 50 such lesions, some coalescing on the face. The best treatment modality for widespread, resistant molluscum contagiosum in HIV is:
opts: Antiretroviral therapy to restore immune function
questions.exp: Widespread, facial, giant, and treatment-refractory molluscum contagiosum in HIV is an AIDS-defining condition (CD4 <50). The most effective long-term strategy is HAART (highly active antiretroviral therapy) which restores CD4 counts and clears molluscum through immune reconstitution. Individual lesion destruction (cryotherapy, TCA) provides temporary control but fails without immune recovery.

questions.q: A 50-year-old female presents with a solitary, firm, skin-colored to yellowish nodule on the upper eyelid. Histology shows large cells with foamy cytoplasm and small peripherally displaced nuclei ('Touton giant cells'). The systemic workup reveals hypercholesterolemia. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Xanthelasma palpebrarum: yellowish, flat or slightly raised plaques on the medial eyelids; Touton giant cells on histology (lipid-laden macrophages); associated with hypercholesterolemia in ~50% of cases. Tuberous xanthomas are over joints. Tendinous xanthomas are on tendons. Eruptive xanthomas are crops of tiny papules associated with hypertriglyceridemia.

questions.q: A 35-year-old male presents with patchy hair loss on the scalp. Dermoscopy reveals yellow dots (follicular plugging with sebum/keratin), black dots (broken hairs), exclamation mark hairs, and short vellus hairs. This dermoscopic pattern is diagnostic of:
questions.exp: Alopecia areata dermoscopy: yellow dots (empty follicles filled with sebum—most sensitive marker), black dots (broken hairs at scalp level, cadaverized hairs), exclamation mark hairs (tapered proximal end, hallmark of activity), and short vellus hairs (regrowth). Trichotillomania has coiled/flame hairs. Tinea capitis has comma hairs and corkscrew hairs.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with progressive darkening of the face, especially the cheeks, forehead, and upper lip, worsening after sun exposure and during her second pregnancy. Wood's lamp examination accentuates the pigmentation. This indicates the pigment is located in:
questions.exp: In Wood's lamp examination (peak emission 365 nm), epidermal pigment (melanin in keratinocytes) is enhanced/accentuated under Wood's lamp. Dermal pigment (melanophages in dermis) is not accentuated (appears unchanged or may even seem to fade). Mixed melasma shows partial accentuation. Clinical significance: epidermal melasma responds better to topical depigmenting agents.
